Caring for the environment

Sporting™ The rules of Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ are clear about this. When a layout is set up, people's safety comes first, and protecting plants and the environment stands right beside it. Shooting at live animals is not allowed.

Where this is in the rules: Chapter 1 · Safety, environment and no live animals

The simplest thing you can do is clean up after yourself. Where there is a bin for empty cases, use it. If you shoot a semi-automatic, it throws each empty case out to the side, so pick yours up when you leave the stand. In both Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting this is a rule, not only good manners.

Targets are changing too. Traditional targets are held together by pitch, a tar-like binder. More makers now offer pitch-free biodegradable targets, which break down more easily in nature. Whether a ground uses them depends on the ground and on local rules.

The FITASC competition rules are written for lead shot (the small lead pellets inside a cartridge). But many countries and regions restrict lead, especially in and around wetlands (marshes, lakes and river banks). There, grounds use steel or another lead-free shot. In the EU, for example, the rule is: since 15 February 2023, no shot with 1% lead or more in wetlands or within 100 m of them. Check the law and the ground's rules before you go. Laws by country, including newer and upcoming bans: Lead, steel and soft iron.

Grounds often lie in beautiful countryside: meadows, woodland edges, hills. Walk only on the permitted paths and take your litter with you. Do not break branches, and drive only where it is allowed.

Many grounds look after their land: they plant trees, collect target fragments and recycle cases. If your club holds such a day, join in. It is part of the culture of the sport and a good way to meet people: Club life and volunteering.

Key points

  • People's safety first, and care for nature right beside it.
  • Empty cases go in the bin; semi-automatic users pick up theirs.
  • Pitch-free targets break down more easily in nature.
  • Where the law restricts lead, grounds use steel: check before you go.

Did you know?

The Sporting™ rules ask layouts to respect hunting ethics. A target should fly at a hunting-like distance. It should not be so close that a real bird would be too damaged to eat, or so far that it would only be wounded.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. What do you do with empty cases after a round?

    1. Leave them where they fall
    2. Put them in the bin provided
    3. Kick them under the stand
    Answer

    Put them in the bin provided

    Cases go in the bin where there is one, and semi-automatic users pick up their ejected cases.

  2. Where might a ground require steel shot?

    1. Where the law restricts lead
    2. Only at Olympic events
    3. Only on very windy days
    Answer

    Where the law restricts lead

    Lead rules depend on the country and the area, often near water; check in advance.

  3. What is special about biodegradable targets?

    1. They are heavier than standard ones
    2. They glow at dusk for visibility
    3. They have no pitch and break down more easily
    Answer

    They have no pitch and break down more easily

    They are made without pitch, so they leave less of it in the soil.
